How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability).

Provenance, kept so that a TRACE Research Object (TRO) declaration of the run can be written later from a stored result (metacheck #404; the helpers are in R/provenance.R). Only when code was run (execute = TRUE): * run_results$started_at, run_results$ended_at: when each run of a script started and ended (ISO 8601, UTC, milliseconds); NA for a script that was not started. A script run again in a later pass has the times of its last run. A TRO uses them for each trov:TransparentResearchPerformance. * run_results$exit_status: the exit status of the process that ran the script (0 = ended normally); NA when the process did not report one (a time limit, or Docker failing to start the container). * artifacts: one row per file, with stage (deposit: as downloaded from the repository, hashed from the downloaded file; before_run: the run folder just before the first script ran, after metacheck’s own changes, such as rewritten paths and unpacked archives; after_run: only the files the scripts made (status new), changed (changed) or removed (removed), as an unchanged file is the one listed before the run), path (relative to the run folder, as valid UTF-8, a byte of another encoding written as <xx>), size (bytes), sha256, mime_type (by extension, NA when unknown), source (the file’s address in the repository, for deposit). The package libraries metacheck installs in the run folder are left out, as are metacheck’s own files there (a script’s runner, and the statistical output it writes in statistical_output/). Files metacheck itself copied or made between passes (see modifications, output_copied, file_placed) show in after_run too. A TRO uses the rows as trov:ResearchArtifacts and each stage as a trov:ArtifactArrangement. * modifications$sha256_before, modifications$sha256_after: the hash of the changed script as downloaded and as it ran; NA when the script is not at the same path in both (a script made from an R Markdown file). * environment: the system that ran the code (trov:TransparentResearchSystem in a TRO): metacheck_version, started_at, ended_at, host (R version, platform, operating system), sandbox, network_isolated (TRUE only when every Docker run had --network none; the process sandbox does not stop the network), internet, timeout_per_script, total_timeout, python_local (the Python run outside Docker and its version), and docker: runs (for each kind of run, r_run, r_install, python_run, python_install, the image and the docker run arguments, such as --network none, --read-only, --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, the process limit and the memory and processor limits) and images (for each image, its ID and digests from docker image inspect, its creation time and the R and Python versions its environment declares).

run_results$checked says what the run of each script shows about the code, in five groups, so that a script that does not reproduce is kept apart from one the check could not test: ran (it ran to the end); code_error (it did not reproduce: it stopped with an error of the code or the deposit, could not be read, or needs a file the deposit does not hold); dependency (a package or program was not available: a package that could not be installed or was not loaded, a program outside R and Python, a system library, or R crashing in a package’s compiled code); time (it did not finish within the time limit for one script, or was not started because the time for all scripts had run out); and not_checkable (it could not be checked automatically: it needs a person, the internet, a key or another setting of the authors’ computer, one platform such as Google Colab, Windows or OpenSAFELY, more memory than the run allows, a file that was not downloaded, a screen, or a program that runs it, or it is a file of a package of the code that Python runs only as a module of that package). It is NA for files run inside another script, files that are not an analysis, files not read, and a Docker failure. summary_table counts each group (repro_ran_n, repro_code_error_n, repro_dependency_n, repro_time_n, repro_not_checkable_n), and the report’s first sentence gives them. The traffic light reflects the static readiness signals by default; a script in code_error that stopped with an error makes it red, as a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure, and a script in one of the other three groups keeps it from being green. Calls that need a screen, which the run does not have (dev.print(), dev.copy2pdf(), dev.copy2eps(), savePlot(), windows(), win.graph(), x11(), quartz(), View()), are replaced before the run by calls that need none, which modifications records as screen_call_replaced. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Representing a structure by a coordinate can be challenging particularly for structures which lack conspicuity, whether due to their small size, lack of contrast, or image artifact. In this paper, we developed a machine learning framework to localize brain targets from the coordinates of salient brain landmarks (i.e., coordinate-to-coordinate) that is agnostic to image contrast. We make use of a validated brain landmark annotation protocol inspired by classical stereotactic methods and a dataset which spans a wide range of MRI field strengths and neurodegenerative diseases. We apply this framework to predict deep brain stimulation targets, achieving an accuracy of 1-1.5 mm validated against expert rater annotations on ultra-high field (UHF) MRI. Results demonstrated comparable localization accuracy on test-retest data acquired using both standard and UHF MRI. Our proposed framework outperformed deformable registration on clinical MRI and performed comparably on multispectral UHF MRI. We deployed our model in the form of a website (stereotaxy.afids.io) and openly release all coordinate data. This framework is agnostic to MRI contrast and offers a method for rapid coordinate localization with applications more broadly in neuroimaging as well as for specialized settings like surgical planning.

1. Introduction

The origins of coordinate-based brain mapping can be traced back to Horsley and Clarke (Horsley & Clarke, 1908), who designed a stereotactic apparatus using Cartesian coordinates to localize brain structures relative to cranial landmarks. Building on this foundation, Jean Talairach (Schaltenbrand et al., 1977; Talairach et al., 1957) leveraged anatomical landmarks, such as the anterior commissure (AC) and posterior commissure (PC), for more refined brain structure localization (i.e., the proportional grid normalization). These early innovations laid the groundwork for population-based brain templates that emerged with the advent of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). For example, the MNI305 template (Collins et al., 1994) aligned 305 individual MRI scans using AC and PC, overcoming the idiosyncrasies of using a single subject brain as a template. Subsequent advances in deformable registration further refined these templates, culminating in modern standards such as the MNI152 space (Fonov et al., 2009), now widely employed for aligning anatomical data. Despite these advances, localizing small, poorly visualized structures with millimetric accuracy remain challenging, particularly when direct anatomical visualization is limited by image resolution, contrast, or artifacts.

Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a stereotactic procedure involving the surgical implantation of electrodes in specific brain structures. It is well established for the management of a wide array of movement disorders such as Parkinson's disease (PD), essential tremor (ET), dystonia, and Tourette's syndrome, as well as for select psychiatric conditions including obsessive-compulsive disorder and treatment-resistant depression (Lozano et al., 2019). Small deviations in electrode position during DBS of the subthalamic nucleus (STN), as an example, result in side-effects including paresthesias, pyramidal symptoms, diplopia, and dysarthria (Buhmann et al., 2017). Meanwhile, suboptimal placement of the electrode by a few millimeters (mm) can lead to reduced clinical outcomes (Anheim et al., 2008) and also put patients at risk for post-operative cognitive decline (Reich et al., 2022). Thus, preoperative localization of DBS targets must approach millimeter-level accuracy for optimal therapeutic benefit.

Achieving the level of accuracy needed in DBS is complicated by the limitations of clinical neuroimaging. Most MRI scanners used in clinical settings operate at 1.5 or 3 Tesla (T), which may not always provide the needed resolution for clear visualization of all DBS targets. Furthermore, patient motion (exacerbated in individuals with movement disorders), suboptimal MRI protocols, and geometric distortions can further degrade image quality (Boutet et al., 2021; Chandran et al., 2016; Lau et al., 2018).

Ultra-high field (UHF; ≥ 7 Tesla) MRI enables clear delineation of small brain regions, since the main magnetic field strength results in enhanced signal-to-noise ratio and tissue contrast that can be exploited to improve spatial resolution (Abosch et al., 2010; Duchin et al., 2012; Lau et al., 2017 Lau et al., , 2020;; Lenglet et al., 2012). However, UHF-MRI systems are not commonly available, posing an obstacle to the widespread use in clinic (Clarke et al., 2020; Middlebrooks et al., 2025). As a result, determining the optimal DBS target still benefits from indirect localization techniques that rely on predefined coordinate spaces.

Existing methods for indirect localization can be grouped into two categories: (1) atlas-based consensus coordinates and (2) atlas-based registration. Atlas-based coordinate approaches describe consensus coordinates of a target relative to the midpoint along the AC-PC line, known as the mid-commissural point (MCP). The MCP is susceptible to intersubject variability, as no single atlasbased consensus coordinate perfectly captures the anatomical differences observed on various populations. Meanwhile, atlas-based (i.e., deformable) registration techniques estimate the deformation field used to propagate atlas labels from a stereotactic space (e.g., MNI) to individual brains. Deformable registration yields errors on the order of 1-5 mm (Abbass et al., 2022; Lau et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2023), with lower quality clinical scans prone to failing thus requiring manual intervention. Neurosurgical planning typically uses gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted MRI (MRI-gad) as the reference image. However, most atlases are derived from data without gadolinium enhancement, so there is no direct one-to-one mapping. This adds complexity to registration that may behave unpredictably (Abbass et al., 2022 (Abbass et al., , 2025) ) and limits the ability to integrate standard neuroimaging workflows (Ogunsanya et al., 2024; Warntjes et al., 2014).

Machine learning (ML) models for automatic localization of brain structures have the potential to offer a faster and more generalizable alternative to deformable registration (Baniasadi et al., 2023; Ren et al., 2025). However, only a limited number of studies have evaluated and adapted ML frameworks to DBS targeting while achieving generalizability on clinical (e.g., MRI-gad) scans (Baniasadi et al., 2023). Furthermore, due to the intensive process of acquiring manual groundtruth labels, many approaches have focused on matching accuracy of well-curated parameters during deformable registration approaches (i.e., training labels generated from quality controlled deformable registration segmentation data) (Baniasadi et al., 2023).

In this study, we validate a coordinate-to-coordinate ML framework to accurately localize brain structures solely from x, y, z coordinates of surrounding anatomical landmarks (see Figure 1). Our target localization approach is dependent only on validated anatomical landmarks (Abbass et al., 2022; Lau et al., 2019), which are reproducible on various MRI field strengths and modalities (Taha et al., 2023). This framework was designed with generalizability and explainability in mind, such that it can be applied to other brain targets while enabling understanding of relationships between predefined landmarks and the targeted brain region, including structures targeted in DBS (e.g., the subthalamic nucleus [STN] and caudal zona incerta [cZI]). Our framework integrates well within the clinical workflow, which already involves preoperative localization of landmarks (e.g., AC and PC). Central to our approach is an open framework, which involves the release of our coordinate data, code, and model in the form of a website ("stereotaxy.afids.io").

2. Methods

>Methods

2.1 Participants

We leverage 202 MRI scans on which we have 6,464 ground truth anatomical landmarks applied in accordance with a validated annotation protocol (Lau et al., 2019) by more than 20 human raters. Below is a breakdown of this data (see Table 1):

The Stereotactic Neurosurgery (SNSX) dataset. This dataset consists of 62 participants (32 healthy controls and 30 scheduled for DBS). Participants were imaged using a 7T head-only MRI scanner (Siemens Magnetom; Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany) at the Centre for Functional and Metabolic Mapping (CFMM) in Western University (REB# 109045). The MRI sequences used for this study were: 1) 3D T1w MP2RAGE and 2) 3D optimized T2w fast-spin echo (T2 SPACE).

The London Health Sciences Centre Parkinson's Disease (LHSCPD) dataset. This dataset consists of a subset (n = 10) of the same participants as in the SNSX dataset, scheduled to undergo DBS at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC; REB# R-17-156). Participants were imaged using a 1.5T MRI scanner (Signa, 1.5T, General Electric, Milwaukee, Wisconsin, USA). The MRI sequence used in this study was a 3D T1w MP2RAGE with gadolinium contrast (termed "MRI-gad" in subsequent sections).

An openly released 3T and 7T (3T-7T) dataset (Chen et al., 2023), consisting of healthy participants (n = 10) imaged using the following sequences: 1) 3D T1w MP2RAGE and 2) 3D T2 SPACE. Participants are imaged at both 3T and 7T (i.e., test-retest).

A subset of a previously released (afids-data) dataset (Taha et al., 2023), which aggregated brain landmark annotations (n = 110) on various populations (healthy, Parkinson's disease, and Alzheimer's disease [AD]). This dataset is independent of the previously mentioned datasets.

A single T1-weighted MNI152NLin2009bAsym and 7T ex vivo template scan (Fonov et al., 2009; Edlow et al., 2019), carrying AFIDs ground-truth annotations, was additionally used to evaluate the sensitivity of STN predictions to AFID annotation variability.

2.2 Coordinate Data Annotation

We employ a previously validated protocol for the annotation of anatomical fiducials (AFIDs; https://afids.github.io/afids-protocol) providing a point-based sampling of multiple brain structures (Lau et al., 2019). In this study, we selected a subset of 16 AFIDs (see Supplementary Figure S1) described by the protocol which (1) circumscribe the midbrain and surrounding structures (e.g., DBS targets) and (2) can be localized within 1.5 mm by expert and novice human raters (Abbass et al., 2022).

AFID Annotations.

All annotations were performed in accordance with the AFIDs protocol via 3D Slicer 4.10 (Fedorov et al., 2012) Rater placements per AFID were averaged to curate the groundtruth coordinates (x, y, and z).

DBS Target Annotations.

All DBS target annotations were performed via 3D Slicer (v.4.10) using the smallest configuration of the paint brush (1 mm) and the pencil drawing tool on 7T T2w imaging. Rater segmentations per subject were selected via majority voting (>50%) and then collapsed to a center of mass constituting the ground truth coordinates (see Lau et al., 2019 for more details). For this work, we annotate the STN, cZI, fasciculus cerebellothalamicus (fct), and red nucleus (RN).

Each scan was annotated by at least two human raters (see Supplementary Table S1 for a breakdown of rater demographic data). The ground truth coordinates were quality controlled (QC) by three raters (AT, JZ, and EC). We provide QC files (*.html format; see Supplementary Attachment A) with accompanying code and ground truth coordinates (*.fcsv) used in this work. Supplementary Attachment B provides an interactive 3D-visualization of all the coordinates and datasets.

2.3 Coordinate Data Processing

An AC-PC alignment was performed followed by centering coordinates at the MCP. Coordinates on the left hemisphere were reflected to the right by inverting the sign of x-coordinate after AC-PC transformation and MCP centering. Thus, each participant constituted two augmented examples. Preliminary analysis using training data was conducted to investigate linear correlations between coordinates and to characterize the variance structure of the concatenated x, y, z AFID coordinates via PCA (Figure 2b-d); this exploratory PCA is descriptive and was not itself used for model training. For ML model training and evaluation, the PCA was instead refit independently within each training partition (see Section 2.4), retaining the top PCs capturing 99% of variance in that partition each time.

2.4 Data Split and Machine Learning

AFID and STN coordinate data of participants from the SNSX dataset were used for ML training (50 participants: 32 HC and 18 PD). Ten further participants from the SNSX dataset (all PD) were assigned to a reserved testing dataset used solely to report the accuracy of our model. These participants were also the same ones from the LHSCPD dataset enabling evaluation of our model on clinical quality 1.5T MRI-gad scans. Finally, the 3T-7T dataset was used for external validation to report prediction accuracy at 3T and 7T MRI.

To select the regression architecture, we screened ten candidate models covering linear, kernelbased, and ensemble methods: Ridge regression (Hoerl & Kennard, 1970), BayesianRidge, ElasticNet, Lasso, partial least squares (PLS), support vector regression with a radial basis function kernel (SVR), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), random forest, a multi-layer perceptron (MLP), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost; Chen & Guestrin, 2016), an ensemble method building on the gradient boosting framework (Friedman, 2001) that can model non-linear relationships. All candidate architectures used the same preprocessing pipeline, with a separate model fitted for each of the x, y, and z coordinates, and hyperparameters were tuned within each training fold using model-specific searches (Supplementary Methods S1.3 and S2). For Ridge, the regularization strength was tuned over a logarithmic grid (α = 10⁻³ to 10⁶, 200 log-spaced values; the deployed model was tuned over a wider grid, 10⁻¹⁰⁰ to 10¹⁰⁰, and its selected values, α = 4.6-11.6, lie inside both ranges). Candidates were compared on cross-validated ED (Supplementary Table S2; Supplementary Figure S2). To examine the trade-off between model simplicity and complexity, we additionally compared Ridge (the simplest regularized linear candidate) with XGBoost (the most flexible non-linear candidate) on per-axis errors from the same cross-validation (Supplementary Figure S3). ML models were trained via a nested cross-validation (CV) strategy to tune hyperparameters and evaluate performance (scikit-learn; Pedregosa et al., 2011). The outer CV loop involved a 4-fold split of all training data (repeated five times with different participant-to-fold assignments) for evaluating and comparing the candidate models and the inner CV loop involved a 3-fold split CV strategy for tuning hyperparameters. To prevent data leakage, we were intentional in our handling of input data, specifically: (1) the folds were curated such that for a given training example (i.e., participant) the left and right hemisphere target labels (e.g., STN) were grouped together (Supplementary Methods S2), preventing left and right labels from appearing separately on training and testing; (2) furthermore, group-based preprocessing (i.e., PCA) was performed independently within each fold. PCA was fit on each fold's training partition augmented with an additional pool of AFID-only scans (the 110 afids-data scans and the two SNSX participants without STN annotations, 112 scans; disjoint from all train/test subjects) for consistency with the deployed model; this retained 24 components at the 99%-variance threshold. Outer-loop errors were used only for model comparison; the selected model was then refit on all training data and evaluated once on the reserved testing datasets (section 3.3; Table 2). We compute the x, y, z mean squared error (MSE) and Euclidean distance (ED) to evaluate models.

2.5 Model Robustness and Comparative Evaluation

Generalization to Other Imaging Modalities.

To investigate model accuracy on clinical imaging, STN coordinate predictions on 1.5T MRI-gad scans were statistically compared to paired groundtruth counterpart 7T MRI-nogad scans. To further demonstrate robustness on both research imaging and external data, we also evaluated model predictions on the 3T-7T dataset. Statistical comparisons were in AC-PC space, and two independent Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were performed across x,y,z MSE and ED with Bonferroni correction (α = 0.05/4). Normality was assessed with the Shapiro-Wilk test; because squared per-axis errors were strongly right-skewed (p < 0.001), all comparisons used non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and are summarized as median [IQR] alongside mean ± SD.

Benchmarking. We performed statistical comparisons between our model and deformable registration for STN localization using our 1.5T MRI-gad dataset (i.e., LHSCPD) and paired 7T-MRI counterpart (i.e., SNSX). The Distal atlas segmentations in MNI space (Chakravarty et al., 2006; Ewert et al., 2018) were warped to native space using presets from a nonlinear deformation framework validated via 11,000 nonlinear warps on more than 100 subjects (Ewert et al., 2019). We applied this framework as implemented in Lead-DBS software (v.3.1; Neudorfer et al., 2023). Groups were compared using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

Robustness to Annotation Variability.

To investigate model dependency on AFID localization error, we evaluated STN prediction accuracy using 38 rater annotations in a common reference space (i.e., MNI). For this analysis, the AFID protocol was applied independently by 10 human raters.

Landmark Prediction Generalizability.

To evaluate whether the coordinate-to-coordinate approach generalizes beyond STN localization, we performed a leave-one-AFID-out analysis using the 16-AFID subset from section 2.2. For each AFID, we treated its coordinates as the prediction target and used the remaining landmarks as predictors. We applied the same participantgrouped nested cross-validation pipeline from section 2.4. We restricted the comparison (see Supplementary Figure S4) to the nine landmarks that define the coordinate space for midbrain and subthalamic targets.

2.6 Extending This Framework to Other Neuromodulation Targets

Having established the accuracy and robustness of the coordinate-to-coordinate framework for STN localization, we next tested whether the same approach would generalize, extending the framework to three additional midbrain structures relevant to DBS planning either as known surgical targets or adjacent features of interest: the caudal zona incerta (cZI), fasciculus cerebellothalamicus (fct), and red nucleus (RN). A single annotation pass therefore would have the potential to support prediction of all four targets addressed in this study (STN, cZI, fct, and RN). The ten candidate regression models described earlier were evaluated at each target, using the same shared preprocessing pipeline, candidate-model roster, and statistical-comparison methodology as the STN model screen (section 2.4; see Supplementary Methods S1), within a Leave-One-Group-Out Cross-Validation (LOGO-CV) framework on the SNSX healthy-control training cohort (32 participants and 32 folds). Given the proof-of-concept scope of this extension and the absence of paired multi-modality or deformable-registration ground truth for these targets, evaluation is restricted to LOGO-CV within the training cohort. Full methodological details are provided in Supplementary Methods S1.

2.7 Model Deployment

Building on the previous open software infrastructure of the AFID project, we deployed our model on a website ("stereotaxy.afids.io"). This enables users to upload their AFID placements as specified by our modified protocol (see Supplementary Figure S1) and receive target coordinate predictions alongside an AC-PC transformation matrix. AFIDs are uploaded in native image space; the website derives the AC-PC/MCP transformation from them, predicts in that space, and returns the STN prediction together with the transformation matrix.

3. Results

>Results

3.1 Rater Curated Data

Demographic data for human raters involved in annotations are made available in Supplementary Table S1. The overall localization error on the subset of 16 AFIDs used in our framework was 0.84 ± 0.31 mm, and rater STN segmentation overlap was 0.78 ± 0.03 (Dice similarity coefficient). Right and left STN segmentations did not differ and were combined in subsequent summaries. Median STN volumes were 136.68 mm³ [IQR 126.43-147.37] in the healthy control (HC) cohort and 126.28 mm³ [IQR 104.69-147.92] in the Parkinson's disease (PD) cohort (p = 0.048; Mann-Whitney U test). Median STN centroid coordinates in MCP space for the HC cohort were x = 10.05 [IQR 9.72, 10.70], y = -0.90 [IQR -1.39, -0.40] and z = -3.27 [IQR -3.52, -2.83] mm, and for the PD cohort were x = 10.29 [IQR 9.32, 10.87], y = -1.02 [IQR -1.31, -0.48] and z = -3.65 [IQR -4.14, -3.05] mm (x: p = 0.93, y: p = 0.91, z: p = 0.002; Mann-Whitney U test). After Bonferroni correction (α = 0.05/4), only the z-coordinate difference remained significant.

3.2 Preliminary Analysis and Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

Pairwise correlations were computed for the x, y, and z coordinates of 16 AFIDs, reduced to 11 unique landmark positions after the hemisphere-mirroring step described in section 2.3 (33 features total; Figure 2a). PCA was employed to reduce the dimensionality of features used for ML model training. In this exploratory, training-only PCA, the top 23 principal components (PCs) captured 99% of the variation in the data (see Figure 2b); the production pipeline, fit with the additional AFID-only pool, retained 24 (Section 2.4). Further exploration of AFID contributions to PCs revealed relatively broad AFID contributions (see Figure 2d). Strong linear associations between AFID coordinates and STN x, y, and z coordinates were observed (Pearson's r = -0.50 to 0.52) in the training data (Figure 2a), supporting the use of a linear regression framework.

3.3 Machine Learning Model Performance

Model Training. Across the 10-model screen (one model per x, y, z coordinate; nested CV), ridge regression ranked first by median ED (0.85 mm; BayesianRidge had a marginally lower mean ED, 0.95 vs. 0.96 mm). After Holm-Bonferroni correction, Ridge was not statistically distinguishable from BayesianRidge, PLS, RandomForest, or ElasticNet, but significantly outperformed SVR, Lasso, XGBoost, KNN, and MLP (Supplementary Table S2; Supplementary Figure S2). In the follow-up comparison with XGBoost, Ridge had lower error (participant-level median ED 0.89 vs. 0.96 mm; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.002; lower error for 72% of participants), with significantly lower x and y but not z errors (Supplementary Figure S3). Given its top rank and its simplicity, Ridge was selected as the final model for predicting STN coordinates in this study.

Model Testing.

Across all testing data (80 STNs), the mean ± SD squared error was 0.45 ± 0.56, 0.66 ± 0.79, and 0.48 ± 0.59 mm² along x, y, and z. The overall median ED was 1.20 mm (IQR: 0.84-1.53 mm; participant-level bootstrap 95% CI for the median: 1.01-1.38 mm; mean ± SD: 1.18 ± 0.44 mm), and 98.8% of STN predictions (79 of 80) were within 2 mm (Table 2). Held-out error was insensitive to the PCA variance threshold (median ED 1.22-1.29 mm for thresholds from 80% to 99.9%) and decreased with increasing training-set size (from 1.48 mm with 8 to 1.22 mm with 50 training participants; Supplementary Figure S5). Cross-validated error was higher in PD than in HC training participants (median ED 1.13 vs. 0.80 mm; Mann-Whitney U test, p = 0.003; Supplementary Results S3), consistent with the higher error on the all-PD held-out test set than in cross-validation.

3.4 Model Generalizability and Comparisons

Validation for Other Imaging Modalities. We evaluated model performance on different imaging modalities by analyzing test-retest data acquired at various field strengths (see Figure 3a-c). Ten participants with both 1.5T MRI-gad (LHSCPD) and 7T MRI-nogad (SNSX), as well as ten participants with both 3T and 7T MRI (3T-7T), were included (see section 2.4). There were no significant differences in x, y, z MSE and ED on the two paired imaging modalities.

Model Comparison and Performance Benchmarking.

We benchmarked our model against deformable registration (see Figure 3d-e). On 1.5T MRI-gad scans, our model statistically outperformed registration (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 20 hemispheres from 10 patients, p < 0.001). Conversely, on multispectral 7T MRI-nogad data (i.e., registration warps computed using both T1 and T2 imaging), no significant difference in performance was observed between registration and our model (p = 0.60).

Robustness to Annotation Variability.

To assess the influence of landmark annotation error on model performance, we examined the relationship between rater localization error and prediction error. A moderate correlation was observed (Pearson r = 0.47; p < 0.001; see Figure 4a-b).

Generalization to other Midbrain Landmarks.

To test whether the coordinate-to-coordinate framework would generalize beyond STN prediction, we performed a leave-one-AFID-out analysis for nine other midbrain landmarks (see section 2.5; Supplementary Figure S4); errors are per-hemisphere Euclidean distances averaged over five repeats of participant-grouped 4-fold crossvalidation (50 participants). AC and PC were localized almost exactly (median ED 0.06 mm; IQR 0.04-0.10) and their errors are identical, since in AC-PC/MCP space each is determined by the other (together they define the AC-PC axis and share a single degree of freedom); they therefore do not test the framework and were excluded from the pooled summary below. Of the remaining seven landmarks, MB (median ED 0.67 mm; IQR 0.47-0.87), IMS (0.68 mm; IQR 0.48-0.93), and SIPF (0.79 mm; IQR 0.54-1.04) were reconstructed most accurately, followed by ICS (1.17 mm; IQR 0.72-1.69), SLMS (1.28 mm; IQR 0.80-1.74), and ILMS (1.38 mm; IQR 1.10-1.84), with PMJ (1.64 mm; IQR 1.08-2.30) the least accurate. Pooled over these seven landmarks, the overall median ED was 1.00 mm (IQR: 0.67-1.53 mm; 700 hemisphere estimates), comparable in magnitude to the inter-rater localization variability previously reported for direct manual AFID annotation (0.36-1.68 mm; Lau et al., 2019). These results indicate that the ridge-regression coordinate-to-coordinate approach is not specific to STN localization and generalizes to reconstructing other midbrain landmarks from the surrounding AFID configuration.

3.5 Generalizability to other deep brain structures

To assess the broader applicability of our framework, we applied the coordinate-to-coordinate approach, including the same model-architecture screen used for the primary target (section 3.3), using an identical candidate roster and preprocessing pipeline (see Supplementary Methods S1). Model benchmarking identified the best-performing architecture for each target: ElasticNet for cZI, RandomForest for fct, and Lasso for RN, though for cZI and fct most other candidates were not statistically distinguishable from the winner after Holm-Bonferroni correction (only KNN and MLP for cZI, and only MLP for fct, were significantly worse), whereas for RN Lasso significantly outperformed Ridge, BayesianRidge, ElasticNet, and MLP but was not distinguishable from PLS, SVR, XGBoost, RandomForest, or KNN (Supplementary Tables S3-S5; Supplementary Figure S2). On LOGO-CV, these top performing models achieved a median ED of 0.81 mm (IQR: 0.56-1.12; mean ± SD: 0.87 ± 0.40), 0.77 mm (IQR: 0.61-1.11; 0.89 ± 0.38), and 0.46 mm (IQR: 0.36-0.70; 0.56 ± 0.28) for the cZI, fct, and RN, respectively (Figure 4c). Complete comparison tables for all 10 candidate models are provided in Supplementary Tables S3 (cZI), S4 (fct), and S5 (RN), with median errors for all architectures in Figure 4d and the corresponding cross-validation error distributions in Supplementary Figure S2.

4. Discussion

We demonstrated that coordinates of predefined brain landmarks can be leveraged to predict the coordinates of other surrounding brain regions with millimetric accuracy. By employing a coordinate-to-coordinate ML framework, our model is agnostic to imaging modality and resolution. Furthermore, we demonstrated that our model outperforms conventional methods when using less optimal clinical scans (e.g., 1.5T MRI-gad) while performing comparably when using multispectral research scans (i.e., 7T MRI with both T1 and T2 contrasts). Finally, we packaged this model in the form of a website, enabling its use in research or clinical contexts.

4.1 Rater Curated Data

AFID Annotations.

Previous AFID validation studies demonstrated millimetric localization in healthy (Lau et al., 2019) and clinical populations (Abbass et al., 2022). The subset of 16 AFIDs in our ML framework was selected for their spatial proximity to the STN, sampling the more predictable morphological features of the midbrain region. Although the complete AFIDs protocol (i.e., 32 AFIDs) typically requires 20-40 minutes following rater training (Lau et al., 2019), we anticipate a substantial reduction in annotation time due to the reduced number of AFIDs used here. To facilitate reproducibility and completeness, we provide a protocol tailored to the 16 AFIDs used in this work, illustrated at true anatomical position on the MNI152NLin2009bAsym template (see Supplementary Attachment C and Supplementary Figure S1).

STN Annotations.

Inter-rater agreement for STN segmentation was strong, with a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.78 ± 0.03. This is consistent with prior manual segmentation studies of the STN and nearby subcortical structures (Camlidag et al., 2014; Miller et al., 2023). Prior work also highlighted that no statistically significant differences were found between left and right STN annotations (Duchin et al.https://paperpile.com/c/rRFrMq/DpZw+aluC 2018; Miller et al., 2023) , justifying their combination in subsequent analyses. On average, the STN volume was reduced in the PD cohort relative to controls (128.03 ± 29.67 mm³ and 136.56 ± 16.24 mm³, p = 0.047). However, this volume difference did not remain statistically significant after Bonferroni correction. Prior studies reported conflicting findingshttps://paperpile.com/c/rRFrMq/6i7v+YdFS with some showing no significant difference in STN volume between PD and HC (Alkemade et al., 2017; Camlidag et al., 2014) , while others reported a reduction in the PD cohort (Colpan & Slavin, 2010; Patriat et al., 2020). We believe a meta-analytic approach is needed for more conclusive findings. Analysis of STN coordinates relative to the MCP revealed a significant inferior shift (i.e., z-axis) in PD patients compared to controls (p = 0.002). This finding may support prior work reporting region-specific morphological changes associated with PD (Kaya et al., 2019). Interestingly, previous work comparing STN coordinates between PD and essential tremor patients reported no significant differences (Duchin et al., 2018) https://paperpile.com/c/rRFrMq/aluC however, essential tremor may not serve as an appropriate baseline for comparison.

4.2 Preliminary Analysis and Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

Our analysis demonstrates that brainstem AFIDs exhibit strong internal spatial correlations, consistent with prior reports of geometrical regularity in this region (Perera et al., 2024). Structures such as the superior lateral mesencephalic sulcus (SLMS), superior interpeduncular fossa (SIPF), and mammillary bodies (MB) were tightly coupled along shared axes, suggesting conserved spatial organization driven by developmental and structural constraints (Párraga et al., 2016). PCA supported this anatomical consistency, with the top five components capturing over 60% of the variance in AFID coordinates. This concentration of variance in a modest number of components reflects meaningful redundancy in the AFID configuration and supports the dimensionality reduction used for downstream ML applications, though the remaining components (23 total for 99% of variance; section 3.2) still contribute non-trivial information preserved for model training. Importantly, variance was broadly distributed over AFIDs rather than dominated by a few landmarks, reflecting coordinated spatial variation across regions. When correlating AFIDs with STN coordinates, SLMS ranked among the top predictors for all axes (strongest |r| per STN axis = 0.38-0.52). The MB and SIPF also demonstrated strong associations (MB: |r| = 0.38-0.47; SIPF: |r| = 0.32-0.48). Univariate correlation does not, however, equal contribution to a multivariate model. In a supervised analysis (Supplementary Figure S6), removing any single landmark changed cross-validated error by at most 0.07 mm, with the largest increases for LVPC, PMJ, LVAC, and SLMS, and nested landmark selection with 4-11 landmarks gave similar error (median ED 0.85-0.90 mm); the ventricular landmarks and PMJ thus contributed as much as SLMS despite weaker univariate correlations, consistent with redundancy among AFIDs. Taken together, these results support a coordinate-based localization approach, leveraging conserved anatomical relationships within the midbrain and diencephalic regions to infer the position of brain targets like the STN.

4.3 Machine Learning Model Performance

Our model achieved a median localization error of 1.20 mm (IQR: 0.84-1.53 mm; bootstrap 95% CI for the median: 1.01-1.38 mm; mean ± SD: 1.18 ± 0.44 mm) on all testing data. This performance is comparable to the localization variability of AFIDs themselves, previously reported to range from 0.36 to 1.68 mm (Lau et al., 2019). For context, a recent study reported a mean interrater centroid localization error of 1.9 ± 1.07 mm between two expert annotators (Miller et al., 2023). A similar coordinate-to-coordinate framework (Engelhardt et al., 2021) achieved a mean error of 1.33 ± 1.64 mm; however, direct comparison is limited, as their target was the active contact of a DBS electrode rather than an anatomically defined structure. Notably, Guo et al. (2007) benchmarked six STN targeting methods and found that a combined anatomical and functional approach yielded a localization error of 1.70 ± 0.7 mm. Clinically, errors under 2 mm are conventionally considered within the range of acceptable (Kremer et al., 2023), particularly when considering the role of intraoperative neurophysiology conventionally to optimize targeting as well as the advantages of modern DBS electrode designs that allow for current steering. A recent multicenter study similarly explored AI-assisted STN-DBS surgical planning using a supervised statistical atlas-based approach, reporting concordance with conventional stereotactic and neurophysiologically guided targeting along the lateral axis in a small clinical cohort (Wu et al., 2026), underscoring growing clinical interest in ML-assisted stereotactic planning more broadly, albeit via a different (statistical-atlas rather than coordinate-regression) approach.

4.4 Model Generalizability and Comparisons

Validation for Other Imaging Modalities. By using paired datasets, we could directly compare predictions for different imaging modalities within the same participants. We found that prediction accuracy was maintained over a range of imaging modalities. These findings align with prior work from our group, which established the feasibility of accurately localizing AFIDs whether the MRI scans are research or clinical quality (Taha et al., 2023). Importantly, comparisons were conducted in AC-PC space, which assumes that independent AFID placements for paired modalities result in equivalent transforms. This approach was necessary due to the lack of ground truth STN segmentations in both the 1.5T MRI-gad and 3T MRI datasets. Despite this potential source of error, our results revealed no statistically significant differences in predicted coordinates.

Model Comparison and Performance Benchmarking.

We employed a commonly used deformable registration pipeline to transform images from stereotactic space to native space. This pipeline employs rigorously optimized parameters (Ewert et al.https://paperpile.com/c/rRFrMq/S7ZH 2019; Schönecker et al., 2009) for diffeomorphic registration from Advanced Normalization Tools (Avants et al., 2008) , incorporating subcortical masks to refine deformation fields and enhance registration accuracy at (Ewert et al., 2019; Schönecker et al., 2009). Our model statistically outperformed registration when using 1.5T MRI-gad scans. MRI-gad scans can be considered a "lowest common denominator" scan employed for neurosurgical planning which provides anatomical detail and additionally the visualization of cerebral vasculature to ensure safe trajectory planning. However, the added gadolinium contrast introduces bias during registration (Abbass et al., 2022 (Abbass et al., , 2025;; Ogunsanya et al., 2024). Prior work comprehensively addressed the added benefit of multispectral imaging (Ewert et al., 2019). In this analysis, we employed sub-millimetric 7T T1w and T2w MRI data. Our model's ability to match registration performance under these conditions highlights its potential utility in settings that lack access to 7T MRI. To our knowledge, our analysis represents the first millimetric account of registration error on MRI-gad scans at the STN. Future investigations should focus on a more comprehensive account of two elements pertaining to registration: (1) isolating and accounting for the MRI-gad bias introduced during registration by employing paired data and (2) evaluating which set of multispectral data provides the best advantage during registration.

Robustness to Annotation Variability.

Not unexpectedly, our model performance was dependent on the accuracy of AFID localization. Indeed, model prediction error was found to increase linearly with AFID localization error (i.e., with every 1 mm of annotation error, prediction accuracy declines by approximately 0.46 mm; see Figure 4b). We believe the robustness to annotation error came from various factors: (1) PCA on input features, which attenuates the impact of isotropic noise by prioritizing structured anatomical variance and down-weighting noisy, low-variance directions; (2) redundancy among AFIDs, where overlapping spatial information allows the model to compensate for small errors in individual landmarks; and (3) regularization, which reduces model sensitivity to noisy features by constraining coefficient magnitudes.

Generalizability to Other Neuromodulation Targets.

Beyond the STN, our framework maintained high millimetric localization accuracy for several additional subcortical targets, demonstrating the broad utility of AFID-based spatial relationships. This generalizability is valuable for targets that present significant visualization challenges with clinical imaging, such as the caudal zona incerta (cZI) and the fasciculus cerebellothalamicus (fct). The cZI cannot always be easily delineated from surrounding structures, surgical localization may rely on indirect, atlas-based targeting. Rather than targeting the cZI directly, neurosurgeons have used two neighboring structures that are highly visible on axial T2w scans (e.g., the red nucleus (RN) and subthalamic nucleus (STN)) as anatomical reference anchors to guide the placement of electrodes (Blomstedt et al., 2010; Plaha et al., 2006). These methods, however, present distinct limitations: both fail to account for interpatient variability, and deformable atlas registration workflows can be computationally expensive and time consuming. Our coordinate-to-coordinate framework offers a fast and light-weight alternative to these indirect and atlas-based approaches (see Section 4.5 for the current validation status of this extension).

4.5 Limitations and Future Directions

A key limitation of our framework is its reliance on the accurate localization of AFIDs. However, prior studies have demonstrated that AFIDs can be placed reliably among a diverse rater demographics and MRI modalities. Furthermore, our detailed open-access placement protocol is designed to make AFID localization more accessible and standardized for a wider user base. Importantly, for our primary use case in DBS, neurosurgeons are accustomed to localization of AFIDs such as the AC and PC as part of routine clinical workflows. Extending these established practices to a broader set of landmarks within the AFID framework is therefore both feasible and well-aligned with current surgical expertise. Applying an automated detection step to input AFID landmarks is a natural next step and would enable an end-to-end pipeline from raw MRI to predicted surgical target. While the shared 16-AFID input is efficient and supported by the observed landmark redundancy (sections 3.4, 4.2), we have not benchmarked it against targetspecific landmark subsets for cZI, fct, or RN; it remains possible that a differently optimized landmark set could further improve accuracy for these secondary targets, and the narrower validation scope applied to them relative to STN should be weighed accordingly when interpreting their reported accuracy. Unlike STN, where model accuracy was confirmed on a reserved test set separate from the cross-validation used for model selection, the reported cZI/fct/RN accuracy reflects the same cross-validation procedure used to select each identified winning architecture, with no independent held-out confirmation; these figures should be interpreted as an optimistic upper bound on true generalization accuracy for these targets rather than a confirmed estimate.

Although our model localizes targets with millimetric accuracy, it is important to recognize that optimal DBS outcomes are typically achieved by targeting the subregions of a given structure (e.g., dorsolateral STN in PD which corresponds to its motor functional territory). This spatial precision is crucial, as the true therapeutic substrate of DBS lies in modulating specific brain networks. In this work, we maintained an anatomically grounded framework as the STN center can be more objectively defined. However, our approach could be adapted to predict coordinates of sub-regions shown to have optimal therapeutic outcomes (Hollunder et al., 2024). Such extensions would allow the model to bridge anatomical and functional targeting strategies. We also emphasize that this framework predicts only the stereotactic target coordinate; it does not address trajectory or entrypoint planning, which includes avoiding vessel or ventricle transgression as well as optimal DBS contact placement relative to the target.

Our current model is only geometry-based, relying on AFIDs without incorporating subject-level information that could enhance prediction accuracy or clinical relevance. Variables such as age, sex, diagnosis, disease severity, or even brain volume may further improve ML-driven localization accuracy. Future iterations of our framework could benefit from a hybrid approach, integrating demographic and clinical covariates alongside anatomical features to better tailor predictions to individual patients and potentially improve outcome prediction. Beyond the training-population and validation-scope limitations of the cZI/fct/RN extension already noted above, these models have also not been evaluated against prospective clinical outcomes, and the optimal active contact location may not coincide with any of these target centroids. Future iterations will expand the framework to include other common DBS targets to serve as a baseline benchmark alongside the fct and cZI models.

While DBS planning often involves implanting electrodes at predefined coordinates, this coordinate-based paradigm has limitations. In broader neuroscience contexts, many structures, particularly white matter pathways such as the fct, may not be fully captured by a single coordinate or point representation. Functional circuits, for instance, span or extend between anatomical locations, and their representation may be better suited to surface-based or tractography-informed models. Nevertheless, a coordinate-based representation of even a part of a white matter pathway can be considered a useful structural anchor in connectivity-based targeting. Future work may benefit from integrating volumetric, functional, or connectivity-based representations to more holistically capture this complexity.

5. Conclusions

In summary, we validated a coordinate-to-coordinate framework for the localization of deep brain structures including the STN and cZI. The model achieved millimetric precision, demonstrated strong generalizability on imaging modalities and additional subcortical landmarks, and outperformed conventional methods for brain structure localization on clinical scans. Its robustness to moderate annotation variability and low computational overhead make it well-suited for integration into neuroimaging and surgical planning pipelines. To facilitate accessibility and reproducibility, we have deployed the model as a user-friendly web application and openly released associated code and coordinate datasets. Figure 1.
